title: PWM Motor Speed Regulation & Direction Control Code
summary: Regulate DC motor velocity with high-frequency Pulse Width Modulation, calculate effective voltage, overcome static friction, and program smooth speed ramps.

steps.title: From On/Off to Variable Velocity
steps.markdownContent:
### Smooth Throttles: Why Robots Need Speed Regulation

Driving a robot with only full-speed and stop is like driving a car with an accelerator pedal that is either slammed to the floor or untouched! Your robot would jerk violently, skid its wheels, fail to dock accurately, and strip gear teeth.

How do you smoothly regulate the speed of a DC motor when your battery provides a fixed voltage (e.g., 9V)?
- You cannot easily vary the battery voltage with variable resistors (potentiometers burn up from heavy current!).
- Instead, engineers use **Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)**!

```
PWM PERIOD T = ~2.04 ms (490 Hz on Arduino Pin 9)

25% DUTY CYCLE (Crawl Speed):
┌─┐       ┌─┐       ┌─┐
│ │       │ │       │ │
┘ └───────┘ └───────┘ └───────  V_effective = 9V * 0.25 = 2.25V

50% DUTY CYCLE (Half Speed):
┌───┐   ┌───┐   ┌───┐
│   │   │   │   │   │
┘   └───┘   └───┘   └───        V_effective = 9V * 0.50 = 4.50V

75% DUTY CYCLE (Cruise Speed):
┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐
│     │ │     │ │     │
┘     └─┘     └─┘     └─        V_effective = 9V * 0.75 = 6.75V
```

### The Magic of Rotor Inertia and Inductance
When you feed PWM into the L293D's Enable pin (Pin 1), you are pulsing the motor supply ON and OFF nearly 500 times per second. The rotor's heavy mechanical inertia and the coil's electrical inductance prevent the motor from stopping between pulses. Instead, the motor responds to the **time-averaged effective voltage**, spinning smoothly at a speed proportional to the duty cycle!

### Beware the Deadband (Static Friction / Stiction)
If you send `analogWrite(enablePin, 20)`, the motor will not spin at all! It will emit a quiet 490Hz humming whine. Why? Mechanical bearings, commutator brushes, and gearbox teeth suffer from **static friction (stiction)**. The motor requires a minimum threshold duty cycle (typically `analogWrite` values of 60 to 80) to break stiction and start moving.

quickCheck.question: How does PWM regulate the speed of a DC motor when the supply voltage is fixed at 9V?
options: It rapidly pulses the 9V supply ON and OFF, varying the duty cycle to alter the effective average voltage
It inserts physical resistors into the circuit using internal relays
It changes the frequency of the microcontroller crystal oscillator
quickCheck.explanation: PWM rapidly switches power ON and OFF, varying the ratio of ON time to period (duty cycle) to control average motor voltage.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Tapping the gas pedal rapidly simulates variable speed without needing a smaller engine!

quickCheck.question: What causes a motor to emit a high-pitched humming whine without rotating when fed very low PWM values (e.g. 20)?
options: The average electrical torque is insufficient to overcome static friction (stiction) and gearbox mechanical drag
The motor's permanent magnets have lost their charge permanently
Low PWM reverses the direction of gravity inside the motor casing
quickCheck.explanation: At low PWM values, the electrical torque cannot overcome the static friction of brushes, bearings, and gears (the motor deadband).
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Think of pushing a heavy box: a tiny nudge won't overcome friction, but a firm push gets it sliding.

steps.title: Duty Cycle Physics & Effective Voltage Calculation

interactiveConfig.title: PWM Duty Cycle and Voltage Relationship

steps.markdownContent:
### Calculating Effective Motor Voltage

The Arduino `analogWrite()` function accepts values from **0** (0% duty cycle, completely OFF) to **255** (100% duty cycle, fully continuous ON):

$$\text{Duty Cycle } (\%) = \left( \frac{\text{PWM Value}}{255} \right) \times 100\%$$

The effective average voltage delivered to the motor ($V_{\text{effective}}$) from a supply voltage ($V_{\text{motor}}$) is:

$$V_{\text{effective}} = V_{\text{motor}} \times \left( \frac{\text{PWM Value}}{255} \right)$$

### Voltage & Throttle Reference Table (9V Battery Supply):

| `analogWrite` Value | Duty Cycle | Effective Voltage | Motor Operating Regime |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **0** | **0%** | **0.00 V** | Fully Stopped (De-energized) |
| **40** | **15.7%** | **1.41 V** | Deadband (Coils hum; static friction holds rotor) |
| **75** | **29.4%** | **2.65 V** | Minimum Reliable Crawl Speed (Stiction overcome) |
| **128** | **50.2%** | **4.52 V** | Half-Throttle Cruising Speed |
| **192** | **75.3%** | **6.78 V** | Fast Maneuver Speed |
| **255** | **100%** | **9.00 V** | Full Throttle Sprint (Maximum RPM and Torque) |

### Why Gradual Speed Ramping Matters
Instantly jumping from PWM 0 to 255 creates massive stall-level inrush currents (1.2A+) that cause severe power rail dips and mechanical shocks. In robotics, engineers always program **software acceleration ramps** to smoothly step the PWM value up over 200–500 milliseconds.

interactiveConfig.question: If a 9V motor is powered through an L293D with analogWrite(enablePin, 128), what is the approximate effective average voltage across the motor?
interactiveConfig.explanation: An analogWrite value of 128 corresponds to a 50% duty cycle (128 / 255 ≈ 0.50). 50% of 9V is approximately 4.5V.

questions.question: If a 9V motor is powered through an L293D with analogWrite(enablePin, 128), what is the approximate effective average voltage across the motor?
questions.explanation: An analogWrite value of 128 corresponds to a 50% duty cycle (128 / 255 ≈ 0.50). 50% of 9V is approximately 4.5V.

questions.question: Why is ramping motor speed gradually with software delays preferred over instantaneous 0 to 255 jumps?
options: It prevents huge current surge spikes, mechanical shock to gear teeth, and power rail brownout dips
It keeps the Arduino sketch from running out of memory
Motors cannot run at 100% speed unless ramped up for 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Smooth acceleration ramps prevent massive inrush stall currents that cause power supply brownout crashes and mechanical gear damage.

questions.question: If your robot motor does not begin spinning until analogWrite() reaches 70, what hardware parameter accounts for this deadband?
options: Static friction (stiction) in the motor bearings, brushes, and mechanical gearbox
The Arduino USB cable has too much electrical resistance
The ATmega328P processor is running at half clock speed
questions.explanation: Stiction is the initial static friction in bearings, brushes, and gears that requires a minimum threshold torque before motion begins.
